{{Short description|Scientific field studying cities as complex systems}}
{{more citations needed|date=April 2025}}

'''Urban scaling'''<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Bettencourt |first1=Luis |last2=West |first2=Geoffrey |date=2010 |title=A unified theory of urban living |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/467912a |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=467 |issue=7318 |pages=912–913 |doi=10.1038/467912a |pmid=20962823 |bibcode=2010Natur.467..912B |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> is an area of research within the study of cities as [[complex system]]s. It examines how various urban indicators change systematically with city size.

The literature on urban scaling was motivated by the success of scaling theory in biology, itself motivated in turn by the success of scaling in physics.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last=Whitfield |first=John |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/ocm67346041 |title=In the beat of a heart: life, energy, and the unity of nature |date=2006 |publisher=Joseph Henry Press |isbn=978-0-309-09681-2 |location=Washington, D.C. |oclc=ocm67346041}}</ref><ref name=":6" /> Crucial insights from scaling analysis applied to a system can emerge from finding [[Power law|power-law function]] relationships between variables of interest and the size of the system (as opposed to finding [[Power-law tail|power-law]] [[probability distribution]]s). Power-laws have an implicit [[self-similarity]] which suggests universal mechanisms at work, which in turn supports the search for fundamental laws.<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Schroeder |first=Manfred Robert |title=Fractals, chaos, power laws: minutes from an infinite paradise |date=2009 |publisher=Dover Publications |isbn=978-0-486-47204-1 |edition=Dover |location=Mineola, N.Y}}</ref> The study of power-laws is closely linked to the study of [[critical phenomena]] in physics, in which [[Emergence|emergent properties]] and [[scale invariance]] are central and organizing concepts. These concepts resurface in the study of complex systems,<ref>{{Cite book |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/3-540-33182-4 |title=Critical Phenomena in Natural Sciences |date=2006 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |isbn=978-3-540-30882-9 |series=Springer Series in Synergetics |location=Berlin/Heidelberg |language=en |doi=10.1007/3-540-33182-4|bibcode=2006cpns.book.....S }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Sornette |first1=Didier |title=Critical Phenomena in Natural Sciences: Chaos, Fractals, Selforganization, and Disorder: Concepts and Tools |last2=Sornette |first2=Didier |date=2006 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-540-33182-7 |edition=2nd |series=Springer series in synergetics |location=Berlin New York}}</ref> and are of particular importance in the urban scaling framework.

The phenomenon of scaling in biology is often referred to as [[allometric scaling]]. Some of these relationships were studied by Galileo (e.g., in terms of the area width of animals' legs as a function of their mass) and then studied a century ago by [[Max Kleiber]] (see [[Kleiber's law]]) in terms of the relationship between [[basal metabolic rate]] and mass. A theoretical explanation of allometric scaling laws in biology was provided by the [[metabolic theory of ecology]].<ref name=":5" />

The application of scaling in the context of cities is inspired by the idea that, in cities, urban activities are [[emergent phenomena]] arising from the interactions of many individuals in close physical proximity. This is in contrast to applying scaling to countries or other social group delineations, which are more ad-hoc sociological constructions. The expectation is that collective effects in cities should result in the form of large-scale quantitative urban regularities that ought to hold across cultures, countries and history. If such regularities are observed, then it would support the search for a general mathematical theory of cities.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Batty |first=Michael |title=The new science of cities |date=2017 |publisher=The MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-53456-7 |edition=First paperback |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts London, England}}</ref>

Indeed, [[Luís M. A. Bettencourt]], [[Geoffrey West]], and Jose Lobo's seminal work<ref name=":1" /> demonstrated that many urban indicators are associated with population size through a [[Power law|power-law]] relationship, in which socio-economic quantities tend to scale superlinearly,<ref name=":2" /> while measures of infrastructure (such as the number of gas stations) scale sublinearly with population size.<ref name=":3" /> They argued for a quantitative, predictive framework to understand cities as collective wholes, guiding urban policy, improving sustainability, and managing urban growth.<ref name=":0" />

The literature has grown, with many theoretical explanations for these emergent power-laws. Ribeiro and Rybski summarized these in their paper "Mathematical models to explain the origin of urban scaling laws".<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Ribeiro |first1=Fabiano L. |last2=Rybski |first2=Diego |date=2023 |title=Mathematical models to explain the origin of urban scaling laws |journal=Physics Reports |volume=1012 |pages=1–39 |doi=10.1016/j.physrep.2023.02.002 |bibcode=2023PhR..1012....1R |issn=0370-1573}}</ref> Examples include Arbesman et al.'s 2009 model,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Arbesman |first1=Samuel |last2=Kleinberg |first2=Jon M. |last3=Strogatz |first3=Steven H. |date=2009-01-30 |title=Superlinear scaling for innovation in cities |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevE.79.016115 |journal=Physical Review E |volume=79 |issue=1 |article-number=016115 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.79.016115|pmid=19257115 |arxiv=0809.4994 |bibcode=2009PhRvE..79a6115A }}</ref> Bettencourt's 2013 model,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bettencourt |first=Luís M. A. |date=2013-06-21 |title=The Origins of Scaling in Cities |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1235823 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=340 |issue=6139 |pages=1438–1441 |doi=10.1126/science.1235823 |pmid=23788793 |bibcode=2013Sci...340.1438B |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Gomez-Lievano et al.'s 2017 model,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gomez-Lievano |first1=Andres |last2=Patterson-Lomba |first2=Oscar |last3=Hausmann |first3=Ricardo |date=2016-12-22 |title=Explaining the prevalence, scaling and variance of urban phenomena |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-016-0012 |journal=Nature Human Behaviour |language=en |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=1–6 |article-number=0012 |doi=10.1038/s41562-016-0012 |issn=2397-3374|arxiv=1604.07876 }}</ref> and Yang et al.'s 2019 model,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=V. Chuqiao |last2=Papachristos |first2=Andrew V. |last3=Abrams |first3=Daniel M. |date=2019-09-16 |title=Modeling the origin of urban-output scaling laws |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevE.100.032306 |journal=Physical Review E |volume=100 |issue=3 |article-number=032306 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.100.032306|pmid=31639910 |arxiv=1712.00476 |bibcode=2019PhRvE.100c2306Y }}</ref> among others (see for a more thorough review of the models <ref name=":4" />). The ultimate explanation of scaling laws observed in cities is still debated.<ref>{{Cite arXiv |last1=Gomez-Lievano |first1=Andres |last2=Fragkias |first2=Michail |date=2024 |title=The benefits and costs of agglomeration: insights from economics and complexity |class=physics.soc-ph |eprint=2404.13178}}</ref><ref>{{Cite arXiv |last1=Ribeiro |first1=Fabiano L. |last2=Netto |first2=Vinicius M. |date=2024 |title=Urban Scaling Laws |class=physics.soc-ph |eprint=2404.02642}}</ref>

Recent studies argue that the scaling of urban indicators reflects how cities are embedded in commuting networks: inter-city commuter flows help explain urban wealth scaling;<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alves |first1=Luís G. A. |last2=Rybski |first2=Diego |last3=Ribeiro |first3=Haroldo V. |title=Commuting network effect on urban wealth scaling |journal=Scientific Reports |year=2021 |volume=11 |issue=1 |page=22918 |doi=10.1038/s41598-021-02327-7  |doi-access=free|pmid=34824348 |pmc=8617032 |arxiv=2111.00827 |bibcode=2021NatSR..1122918A }}</ref> inter-city firm connections help explain why some cities outperform population-based predictions of economic output and innovation;<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Victoria C. |last2=Jackson |first2=James J. |last3=Kempes |first3=Chris P. |title=Inter-city firm connections and the scaling of urban economic indicators |journal=PNAS Nexus |year=2024 |volume=3 |issue=11 |article-number=pgae503 |doi=10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae503 |doi-access=free |pmid=39575096 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Liang |first1=Xun |last2=Hidalgo |first2=César A. |last3=Balland |first3=Pierre-Alexandre |last4=Zheng |first4=Siqi |last5=Wang |first5=Jianzhong |title=Intercity connectivity and urban innovation |journal=Computers, Environment and Urban Systems |year=2024 |volume=109 |article-number=102092 |doi=10.1016/j.compenvurbsys.2024.102092 |arxiv=2406.14681 |bibcode=2024CEUS..10902092L }}</ref> disease incidence across cities is also shaped by the strength of commuting ties;<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Loureiro |first1=Natália A. |last2=Neto |first2=Carlos R. |last3=Sutton |first3=Jon |last4=Perc |first4=Matjaž |last5=Ribeiro |first5=Haroldo V. |title=Impact of inter-city interactions on disease scaling |journal=Scientific Reports |year=2025 |volume=15 |issue=1 |page=498 |doi=10.1038/s41598-024-84252-z  |doi-access=free|pmid=39748086 |pmc=11696764 }}</ref> and commuter inflows also contribute to the scaling of urban crime.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Puttock |first1=Simon |last2=Barros |first2=Umberto |last3=Pinheiro |first3=Diego |last4=Oliveira |first4=Marcos |title=Larger cities, more commuters, more crime? The role of inter-city commuting in the scaling of urban crime |journal=Crime Science |year=2025 |volume=14 |article-number=19 |doi=10.1186/s40163-025-00264-8  |doi-access=free|hdl=1871.1/ee4d967a-d567-4606-89f6-8adb7ffcb48d |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

== Pioneering work ==

=== Santa Fe Institute's cities group ===
Source:<ref>{{Cite web |title=Projects: Cities, scaling, & sustainability {{!}} Santa Fe Institute |url=https://santafe.edu/research/projects/cities-scaling-sustainability |access-date=2024-10-16 |website=www.santafe.edu |language=en}}</ref>

* Luis Bettencourt, [[Geoffrey West]], Jose Lobo, and their colleagues at the [[Santa Fe Institute]], conducted seminal work on urban scaling.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Bettencourt |first1=Luis M.A. |last2=Lobo |first2=José |last3=Strumsky |first3=Deborah |date=2007 |title=Invention in the city: Increasing returns to patenting as a scaling function of metropolitan size |journal=Research Policy |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=107–120 |doi=10.1016/j.respol.2006.09.026 |issn=0048-7333}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pumain |first1=Denise |last2=Paulus |first2=Fabien |last3=Vacchiani-Marcuzzo |first3=Céline |last4=Lobo |first4=José |date=2006-07-05 |title=An evolutionary theory for interpreting urban scaling laws |url=https://journals.openedition.org/cybergeo/2519 |journal=Cybergeo: European Journal of Geography |language=en |doi=10.4000/cybergeo.2519 |issn=1278-3366|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bettencourt |first1=L. M.A. |last2=Lobo |first2=J. |last3=West |first3=G. B. |date=2008-06-01 |title=Why are large cities faster? Universal scaling and self-similarity in urban organization and dynamics |journal=The European Physical Journal B |language=en |volume=63 |issue=3 |pages=285–293 |doi=10.1140/epjb/e2008-00250-6 |bibcode=2008EPJB...63..285B |issn=1434-6036}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Bettencourt |first1=Luís M. A. |last2=Lobo |first2=José |last3=Helbing |first3=Dirk |last4=Kühnert |first4=Christian |last5=West |first5=Geoffrey B. |date=2007-04-24 |title=Growth, innovation, scaling, and the pace of life in cities |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=104 |issue=17 |pages=7301–7306 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0610172104 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=1852329 |pmid=17438298|bibcode=2007PNAS..104.7301B }}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Kühnert |first1=Christian |last2=Helbing |first2=Dirk |last3=West |first3=Geoffrey B. |date=2006 |title=Scaling laws in urban supply networks |journal=Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and Its Applications |volume=363 |issue=1 |pages=96–103 |doi=10.1016/j.physa.2006.01.058 |bibcode=2006PhyA..363...96K |issn=0378-4371}}</ref> They identified consistent scaling laws across cities worldwide, showing that larger cities tend to be more innovative and productive but also face challenges such as increased crime rates and disease spread.
* Their research demonstrated that many urban characteristics, from GDP to infrastructure, follow predictable scaling patterns. For example, they found that economic indicators typically have a superlinear scaling exponent (<math>\beta\approx1.15</math>), while infrastructure shows sublinear scaling (<math>\beta\approx0.85</math>).
* They started the research field of urban scaling with the explicit goal of understanding the power-law relationship between aggregate urban metrics and population size.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=West |first=Geoffrey B. |title=Scale: the universal laws of growth, innovation, sustainability, and the pace of life in organisms, cities, economies, and companies |date=2017 |publisher=Penguin Press |isbn=978-1-59420-558-3 |location=New York}}</ref>

=== Economics ===
Some early studies in economics can be seen to have contributed to early stages of the urban scaling literature (unintendedly) by their analyses of how economic outcomes change with population size. One such study is Sveikauskas' 1975 "The productivity of cities",<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sveikauskas |first=Leo |date=1975 |title=The Productivity of Cities |url=https://academic.oup.com/qje/article-lookup/doi/10.2307/1885259 |journal=The Quarterly Journal of Economics |volume=89 |issue=3 |pages=393–413 |doi=10.2307/1885259|jstor=1885259 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> in which he reports a positive association between the average productivity of workers and city population size.

Today, [[urban economics]] is a thriving field within economics, focused on understanding cities.<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last=Glaeser |first=Edward L. |title=Cities, Agglomeration, and Spatial Equilibrium |date=2008 |publisher=Oxford University Press, Incorporated |isbn=978-0-19-929044-4 |series=The Lindahl Lectures |location=Oxford}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Quigley |first=John M. |chapter=Urban Economics |date=2008 |title=The New Palgrave Dictionary of Economics |pages=1–7 |editor-last=Palgrave Macmillan |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/10.1057/978-1-349-95121-5_1616-2 |access-date=2025-08-08 |place=London |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan UK |language=en |doi=10.1057/978-1-349-95121-5_1616-2 |isbn=978-1-349-95121-5|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> The organizing idea for urban economists is the concept of "[[Economies of agglomeration|agglomeration economies]]", which refers to the causal underpinnings of the benefits and costs that accrue when people come together in physical space.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rosenthal |first1=Stuart S. |last2=Strange |first2=William C. |date=2020-08-01 |title=How Close Is Close? The Spatial Reach of Agglomeration Economies |journal=Journal of Economic Perspectives |language=en |volume=34 |issue=3 |pages=27–49 |doi=10.1257/jep.34.3.27 |issn=0895-3309|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Citation |last1=Duranton |first1=Gilles |chapter=Chapter 48 Micro-foundations of urban agglomeration economies |date=2004 |title=Handbook of Regional and Urban Economics |volume=4 |pages=2063–2117 |chapter-url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1574008004800051 |access-date=2025-08-08 |publisher=Elsevier |language=en |doi=10.1016/s1574-0080(04)80005-1 |isbn=978-0-444-50967-3 |last2=Puga |first2=Diego|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> Of particular relevance for understanding the phenomenon of urban scaling, a big body of literature in urban economics investigates the so-called "urban wage premium", which is the empirical observation that nominal wages tend to be larger in larger cities.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Puga |first=Diego |date=February 2010 |title=The Magnitude and Causes of Agglomeration Economies |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9787.2009.00657.x |journal=Journal of Regional Science |language=en |volume=50 |issue=1 |pages=203–219 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9787.2009.00657.x |bibcode=2010JRegS..50..203P |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Heuermann |first1=Daniel |last2=Halfdanarson |first2=Benedikt |last3=Suedekum |first3=Jens |date=April 2010 |title=Human Capital Externalities and the Urban Wage Premium: Two Literatures and their Interrelations |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0042098009352363 |journal=Urban Studies |language=en |volume=47 |issue=4 |pages=749–767 |doi=10.1177/0042098009352363 |bibcode=2010UrbSt..47..749H |issn=0042-0980|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rosenthal |first1=Stuart S. |last2=Strange |first2=William C. |date=September 2008 |title=The === Sociology ===
The field of sociology has also investigated the relationship between socioeconomic variables and the size and density of populations.

For example, [[Émile Durkheim]], a French sociologist, highlighted the sociological impacts of [[population density]] and growth in his 1893 dissertation, "The Division of Labour in Society." In his work, Durkheim emphasized the collective social effects of population. He proposed that an increase in population leads to more social interactions, resulting in competition, specialization, and eventually conflict, which then necessitates the development of social norms and integration. This concept, known as "dynamic density," was later expanded by American sociologist [[Louis Wirth]], particularly in the context of urban settings. However, it wasn't until the 1970s that these ideas were translated into (sociological) mathematical models, sparking debates among sociologists about the complexities of urban agglomeration.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mayhew |first1=Bruce H. |last2=Levinger |first2=Roger L. |date=1976 |title=Size and the Density of Interaction in Human Aggregates |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/226271 |journal=American Journal of Sociology |language=en |volume=82 |issue=1 |pages=86–110 |doi=10.1086/226271 |bibcode=1976AmJSo..82...86M |issn=0002-9602|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Milgram |first=Stanley |title=The experience of living in cities: A psychological analysis. |date=1970 |work=Psychology and the problems of society. |pages=152–173 |editor-last=Korten |editor-first=Frances F. |url=https://content.apa.org/books/10042-011 |access-date=2024-07-24 |place=Washington |publisher=American Psychological Association |language=en |doi=10.1037/10042-011 |editor2-last=Cook |editor2-first=Stuart W. |editor3-last=Lacey |editor3-first=John I.|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kasarda |first=John D. |date=1974 |title=The Structural Implications of Social System Size: A Three-Level Analysis |journal=American Sociological Review |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=19–28 |doi=10.2307/2094273|jstor=2094273 }}</ref>

Critics like [[Claude S. Fischer]] argued that mathematical models oversimplified the reality of social interactions in cities. Fischer contended that these models assumed urbanites interact randomly, akin to marbles in a jar, which fails to capture the nuanced and localized nature of city life. He pointed out that most city dwellers have limited interactions within their neighborhoods and rarely venture into other parts of the city, contradicting the notion that social interactions scale uniformly with population size. Fischer's criticism emphasized the need for a deeper understanding of social systems, beyond mere quantitative models.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fischer |first=Claude S. |date=1977 |title=Comment on Mayhew and Levinger's "Size and the Density of Interaction in Human Aggregates" |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/226556 |journal=American Journal of Sociology |language=en |volume=83 |issue=2 |pages=452–455 |doi=10.1086/226556 |issn=0002-9602|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Criticisms of urban scaling theory ==
Since the formulation of the urban scaling hypothesis, several researchers from the complexity field have criticized the framework and its approach. These criticisms often target the statistical methods used, suggesting that the relationship between economic output and city size may not be a [[power law]]. For instance, Shalizi (2011)<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Shalizi |first=Cosma Rohilla |title=Scaling and Hierarchy in Urban Economies |date=2011-04-07 |class=stat.AP |eprint=1102.4101 }}</ref> argues that other functions could fit the relationship between urban characteristics and population equally well, challenging the notion of scale invariance. Bettencourt et al. (2013)<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Bettencourt |first1=Luis M. A. |title=The hypothesis of urban scaling: formalization, implications and challenges |date=2013-01-24 |last2=Lobo |first2=Jose |last3=Youn |first3=Hyejin|class=physics.soc-ph |eprint=1301.5919 }}</ref> responded that while other models might fit the data, the power-law hypothesis remains robust without a better theoretical alternative.

Other critiques by Leitão et al. (2016)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Leitão |first1=J. C. |last2=Miotto |first2=J. M. |last3=Gerlach |first3=M. |last4=Altmann |first4=E. G. |date=2016 |title=Is this scaling nonlinear? |journal=Royal Society Open Science |language=en |volume=3 |issue=7 |article-number=150649 |doi=10.1098/rsos.150649  |doi-access=free|issn=2054-5703 |pmc=4968456 |pmid=27493764|arxiv=1604.02872 |bibcode=2016RSOS....350649L }}</ref> and Altmann (2020)<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Altmann |first=Eduardo G. |date=2020-12-07 |title=Spatial interactions in urban scaling laws |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=15 |issue=12 |article-number=e0243390 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0243390 |doi-access=free |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=7721189 |pmid=33284830|arxiv=2006.14140 |bibcode=2020PLoSO..1543390A }}</ref> pointed out potential misspecifications in the statistical analysis, such as incorrect distribution assumptions and the independence of observations. These concerns highlight the need for theory to guide the choice of statistical methods. Additionally, the issue of defining city boundaries raises conceptual challenges. Arcaute et al. (2015)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Arcaute |first1=Elsa |last2=Hatna |first2=Erez |last3=Ferguson |first3=Peter |last4=Youn |first4=Hyejin |last5=Johansson |first5=Anders |last6=Batty |first6=Michael |date=2015 |title=Constructing cities, deconstructing scaling laws |journal=Journal of the Royal Society Interface |language=en |volume=12 |issue=102 |article-number=20140745 |doi=10.1098/rsif.2014.0745 |issn=1742-5689 |pmc=4277074 |pmid=25411405}}</ref> and subsequent studies showed that different boundary definitions yield different scaling exponents, questioning the premise of agglomeration economies. They suggest that models should consider the intra-city composition of economic and social activities rather than relying solely on aggregate measures.

Another criticism of the urban scaling approach relates to the over-reliance on averages in measuring individual-level quantities such as average wages, or average number of patents produced. [[Complex system]]s, such as cities, exhibit distributions of their individual components that are often [[Heavy-tailed distribution|heavy-tailed]]. [[Heavy-tailed distribution]]s are very different from [[normal distribution]]s, and tend to generate [[Extreme value theory|extremely large values]]. The presence of extreme outliers can invalidate the [[law of large numbers]], making averages unreliable. Gomez-Lievano et al. (2021)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gomez-Lievano |first1=Andres |last2=Vysotsky |first2=Vladislav |last3=Lobo |first3=José |date=2021 |title=Artificial increasing returns to scale and the problem of sampling from lognormals |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/2399808320942366 |journal=Environment and Planning B: Urban Analytics and City Science |language=en |volume=48 |issue=6 |pages=1574–1590 |doi=10.1177/2399808320942366 |issn=2399-8083|arxiv=1807.09424 |bibcode=2021EnPlB..48.1574G }}</ref> showed that in log-normally distributed urban quantities (such as wages), averages only make sense for sufficiently large cities. Otherwise, artificial correlations between city size and productivity can emerge, misleadingly suggesting the appearance of urban scaling.
